stem.en: The picture shows a polished celt and a ring stone beside a flaked handaxe. Which feature marks a stone tool as Neolithic rather than Palaeolithic?

image.alt: A drawing that compares tools: on the left a polished stone celt and a perforated ring stone, on the right a flaked pear-shaped handaxe.

text.en: It is smaller, because Neolithic tools are always smaller than Palaeolithic ones.

feedback.en: Middle Palaeolithic flakes and Mesolithic microliths are already smaller than a celt, so size does not mark the period.

text.en: It is made of a harder rock than Palaeolithic tools.

feedback.en: The rock is not the mark. Both periods used hard stone, and the difference is how it was shaped.

text.en: It is found in the same layer as animal bones.

feedback.en: Animal bones also lie beside Palaeolithic tools, so where a tool was found does not mark the period.

text.en: It is ground and polished for clearing and tilling, not only flaked for cutting.

explanation.en: A Neolithic stone tool is made for land and crop work. It is shaped by grinding and polishing, as a celt shows. Size, rock and the bones around it do not mark the period.

hints.en: Ask how the surface of each tool was shaped, and what work it was shaped for.
